title: Topical Applications
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Skin Barrier Function
headings.content: Topical drug administration involves applying medications directly to body surfaces, primarily the skin, mucous membranes, eyes, ears, and nose, to achieve a localized therapeutic effect. The primary anatomical barrier to percutaneous drug absorption is the **stratum corneum**, the outermost layer of the epidermis. Often conceptualized as a brick-and-mortar structure, this layer consists of dead, keratin-filled corneocytes (the bricks) embedded in a lipid-rich intercellular matrix (the mortar). For a topically applied drug molecule to exert its systemic or deep tissue effects, it must successfully partition out of its vehicle, diffuse across this dense stratum corneum, and traverse the viable epidermis and dermis to reach the cutaneous microcirculation.

headings.title: Types of Topical Formulations and Vehicles
headings.content:
The vehicle carrying a topical medication drastically influences its release rate, absorption, and clinical efficacy. Choosing the correct vehicle depends on the pathological state of the skin—whether it is acute and weeping, or chronic, thick, and scaly.

- **Ointments**: Greasy, occlusive preparations with high oil content and low water content. They trap moisture, enhance drug penetration, and suit dry, lichenified skin lesions.
- **Creams**: Emulsions of oil and water that spread easily and leave little residue. They work well on weeping lesions or intertriginous areas where occlusion causes maceration.
- **Lotions**: Pourable suspensions or emulsions with a high water content. They cool inflamed skin and apply easily to hair-bearing regions.
- **Gels**: Semisolid aqueous systems thickened with agents like carbomers. They liquefy upon contact with skin, drying to form a thin, non-greasy film ideal for acne or oily skin.
- **Transdermal Patches**: Specialized matrix or reservoir systems engineered to deliver precise, systemic drug doses continuously over extended periods.

headings.title: Specialized Mucosal and Sensory Organ Applications
headings.content:
Topical therapy extends beyond the skin to sensitive mucosal tissues and sensory organs, each demanding distinct administration techniques. Ophthalmic formulations—eye drops and ointments—must be sterile and isotonic to prevent tissue damage and severe infection. When administering eye drops, instilling them into the lower conjunctival sac while avoiding contact between the dropper tip and the eyelashes prevents contamination. Gentle pressure applied to the inner canthus (punctal occlusion) for one minute post-instillation minimizes systemic absorption through the highly vascular nasal mucosa.

Otic preparations for the ear canal require careful temperature management; cold ear drops induce severe vertigo via vestibular stimulation. Pulling the pinna upward and backward in adults (or downward and straight back in infants) straightens the ear canal. Nasal sprays demand proper nozzle positioning to direct the spray away from the nasal septum, preventing local mucosal irritation, epistaxis, and potential septal perforation.

headings.title: Patient Assessment and Safe Administration Techniques
headings.content:
Before applying any topical medication, a comprehensive skin and mucosal assessment must be performed. Inspect the target area for integrity, hydration status, cleanliness, and signs of active infection or breakdown. Assess the patient for known drug allergies and ensure the correct pharmacological agent matches the prescribed anatomical site.

Hand hygiene and the use of non-sterile gloves protect both the patient and the healthcare provider, especially when handling potent corticosteroids or cytotoxic topicals. Cleansing the skin gently with mild soap and water removes crusts, exudates, and residual medication from previous applications. Patting the area dry preserves a slight moisture barrier that aids drug diffusion. Apply creams and ointments in thin, even layers following the direction of hair growth to prevent follicular occlusion and subsequent folliculitis. For transdermal patches, rotate the application site strictly to prevent local skin irritation, and always remove the old patch before applying a new one to avoid accidental toxic overdose.

headings.title: Adverse Effects and Complications
headings.content:
While topical therapies localize drug action and limit systemic toxicity compared to oral routes, adverse reactions remain a clinical risk. Local complications include contact dermatitis, chemical burns, pruritus, and secondary skin infections. Prolonged application of potent topical corticosteroids can cause local skin atrophy, striae formation, telangiectasia, and hypopigmentation.

Systemic adverse effects occur when significant amounts of a drug cross the stratum corneum and enter the systemic circulation. High-potency corticosteroids applied over large surface areas or under occlusive dressings can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. Systemic absorption of topical antimicrobials or anesthetics can precipitate allergic hypersensitivity reactions, ranging from mild urticaria to full-blown anaphylaxis.

headings.title: Patient Education and Concordance in Home Care
headings.content:
Long-term success in dermatological therapy heavily relies on patient education and adherence. Patients often mismanage topical medications by applying overly thick layers under the misconception that more medication works faster. Demonstrating the proper dosing amount—such as the fingertip unit, where the amount squeezed from a tube from the fingertip to the first joint covers an area equivalent to two adult palms—prevents drug waste and systemic toxicity.

Clear instructions regarding handwashing after application prevent accidental transfer of medication to the eyes or mouth. Nurses must encourage patients to report worsening redness, burning, or lack of therapeutic response promptly. Addressing financial constraints, complex dosing schedules, and cosmetic acceptability ensures patients maintain concordance with their prescribed regimen.
